opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the METR work is one of the more useful things we have, because it gives us a single, fairly interpretable number we can track over time: how long a task, measured by how long it takes a skilled human, an AI system can complete with some reliability, say 50 percent. And the striking finding is that this horizon has been doubling roughly every seven months, maybe faster recently. So it's very tempting to draw the line forward and say: well, when it reaches a working month or a working year, that's AGI, and here's the date.

But there are several places where that extrapolation gets shaky.

The first is the threshold itself. What time horizon corresponds to AGI? A week? A month? A career? Because the trend is exponential, being off by a factor of ten in the threshold only moves the date by a few doublings. That's the reassuring part. But we're also quite unsure what counts, and for transformative effects you might need very high reliability, not 50 percent. The gap between 50 percent and 99 percent success horizons is large, and it's not clear that gap closes at the same rate.

The second is the task distribution. These are mostly software and research-engineering tasks that are well specified, self-contained, and automatically checkable. That's exactly where you'd expect AI to do best. Real-world work is messier: vague goals, long feedback loops, coordination with other people, physical context. So a system might have a month-long horizon on benchmark-style tasks while being much weaker on the tasks that actually matter for the economy or for science. The trend line on the benchmark might not transfer.

The third is the trend itself. We have a handful of years of data. The doubling time has already shifted, and it depends heavily on what inputs are driving it. A lot of recent progress has come from scaling up reinforcement learning and inference compute, and I've argued those may have worse scaling properties than pretraining did. You get gains, but each increment can cost much more. If compute costs, or the willingness to spend, start to bind, the doubling time could stretch. Conversely, if AI starts accelerating AI research, it could shorten. Exponentials are very sensitive to small changes in the rate when you project years ahead.

And finally there's a cost dimension that the headline graph hides. A system that can do a month-long task but needs enormous inference spending to do it is not the same as one that does it cheaply. AGI in an economically meaningful sense requires being competitive with human labour on price, not just possible in principle.

So putting that together: the METR trend is real evidence and it should move people toward thinking capable systems could arrive within years rather than decades. But the uncertainty in the threshold, the reliability level, the task generalisation, and the future doubling rate all compound. You end up with a distribution that's spread over maybe a decade or more, not a confident date. I think the honest takeaway is that it narrows things somewhat and raises the plausibility of short timelines, while still leaving a lot of room either way.

r001.rationale: The response notes that METR measures tasks at about 50% reliability and that higher reliability may require a much longer horizon, but it does not state that passing an eight-hour task half the time fails to imply reliable full workdays every day.

r002.rationale: It says the AGI threshold is unknown, asking whether it is a week, month, or career, and explains that this uncertainty makes the extrapolated date shaky.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to say is that I think the METR work is genuinely one of the most useful empirical results we've had in forecasting AI capabilities. They've found this remarkably clean trend: the length of tasks that frontier models can complete, measured in how long those tasks would take a skilled human, has been doubling roughly every seven months. And the natural move is to just extend that line and say, well, at some point the horizon reaches a working week, a month, a year, and that's when we've got something like AGI.

But when you look closely at what's actually being measured, the picture gets quite a bit murkier.

The most important thing is the success rate. That headline number is the horizon at which the model succeeds fifty percent of the time. And fifty percent is really quite a low bar for most real work. If you want a system that you can actually hand a job to, you probably care about something closer to ninety-nine percent reliability, and the horizon at that threshold is dramatically shorter. In the METR data, going from fifty percent to eighty percent success cuts the horizon by something like a factor of four or five. And we don't have good data on what happens at ninety-five or ninety-nine percent, but the structure of the curve suggests it keeps collapsing. So the question of when AGI arrives depends enormously on which reliability level you think counts. That alone can shift your date by years.

The second issue is that the tasks themselves are a particular kind of task. They're mostly software engineering and research-style problems that are self-contained, well specified, and have a clear automated check for whether you succeeded. That's exactly the kind of work that's easiest to train on and easiest to measure. It's not obvious the same trend holds for messy tasks where the goal is ambiguous, where you need context that isn't written down anywhere, or where the feedback is slow and noisy. The trend might be real for one slice of cognitive work and look quite different elsewhere.

Then there's the question of the human baseline. The horizon is defined in terms of how long humans take. But humans and models fail in quite different ways. A model with a two-hour horizon isn't a person who can work for two hours; it's a system that does certain two-hour tasks well and falls apart on certain ten-minute tasks that a person would find trivial. So translating a time horizon into a claim about general capability requires an assumption that these profiles converge, and I'm not sure they do.

And finally, there's the plain question of whether an exponential trend continues. The doubling time has possibly even sped up recently, which some people read as evidence of acceleration, but short trends are noisy and we've seen inflection points before. The trend is driven by inputs like compute, data, and research effort, and those inputs can't grow at the current pace indefinitely. It's hard to know whether we're looking at the middle of a long exponential or the steep part of an S-curve.

So I'd put it this way. The METR horizons give you a real trend, and they make it very hard to argue that transformative systems are decades away. But the same data is consistent with fifty-percent-reliable agents on narrow tasks in a couple of years and with genuinely general, dependable systems still being much further off. The uncertainty isn't because the measurement is bad. It's because the gap between what's being measured and what we actually mean by AGI is large, and the data doesn't tell us how fast that gap closes.

r001.rationale: The response says the headline horizon reflects only 50% success, calls that too unreliable for most real work, and contrasts it with the much higher reliability needed to hand a system a job. That conveys that a half-success threshold does not establish dependable work performance.

r002.rationale: The response says the measured trend is separated from what we mean by AGI and that the data does not show how quickly that gap closes, so extrapolating the trend does not determine an AGI date.

astra-6.text:
Well, even if we knew exactly how that trend was going to continue, there’s still a question about what level on the graph would correspond to AGI. Is it being able to do a task that takes a human a day? A month? A year? We don’t have a settled answer to that, and on an exponential trend, that uncertainty can translate into quite a large difference in dates.

And the time it takes a human to do a task isn’t a complete measure of its difficulty for an AI. A long task might just involve repeating a fairly straightforward operation, while a short one might require a genuinely new insight. So success on longer tasks in the benchmark doesn’t automatically establish that a system can do the full range of human cognitive work.

I think these measurements are useful evidence about progress. But extrapolating the line and identifying the arrival of AGI are two different steps. You need an argument connecting the measured capability to AGI, as well as an argument that the trend will continue.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about which task length would correspond to AGI and says longer-task success does not establish the full range of cognitive work. It does not state that succeeding on an eight-hour task half the time fails to imply reliable performance of a full workday’s tasks every day.

r002.rationale: It says that even if the trend continued exactly, the level on the graph corresponding to AGI is unknown, naming a day, month, or year-long task as possible thresholds; this makes the AGI date uncertain.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think these results are very interesting, but there are several steps between observing that trend and getting a date for AGI. One is whether the trend continues. Another is what exactly the measured time horizon tells us. It’s the time a human would take on tasks that a system can complete at a particular success rate. It isn’t a measure of how long the system can act reliably in any environment.

And then there’s the question of which tasks are represented. A system might become very good at long software tasks while still having important weaknesses elsewhere. Even within software, a task with a clear objective and an easy way to check success can be quite different from an open-ended project where you have to work out what matters.

So, even if you knew when the curve would cross a month or a year, you’d still need an argument connecting that milestone to AGI. The trend is evidence that we should take rapid progress seriously. But the precision of a fitted curve shouldn’t be mistaken for precision about when we’ll get general intelligence.

r001.rationale: The candidate defines the measured horizon by task duration and success rate, but does not mention an eight-hour task, succeeding half the time, or reliability across a full workday every day.

r002.rationale: The candidate says that even knowing when the curve crosses a month or year, an argument is still needed to connect that milestone to AGI, clearly conveying that the AGI-relevant threshold is unknown.
